sources.title: 了解 Gemini Notebook (Learn about Gemini Notebook)
directly_supported_observations: System provides inline citations from uploaded sources (PDF, websites, YouTube videos, audio files, Google Docs, Google Slides)
Gemini Notebook designed to answer questions based on information provided in uploaded sources
System distinguishes three failure modes: safety flagging, unclear phrasing, no relevant information in sources
For Workspace/Education users: uploaded content NOT used for AI training; NOT subject to human review
Chinese official page accessed; product may be called Gemini Notebook or NotebookLM
design_implications: Source-bound AI architecture demonstrated as product feature
Material scope enforcement requires explicit failure mode messages
Citation mechanism presented as accuracy/transparency/trust feature
File upload pattern establishes basic course boundary
limitations_and_non_inferences: No learning effectiveness evidence provided
No pedagogical action specification
No learner modeling capability described
Product status uncertain (naming: Gemini Notebook vs. NotebookLM)
English documentation not accessible; relying on Chinese official page
sources.notes: Product documentation in Chinese; describes feature set without effectiveness claims

sources.title: Using Study Mode in ChatGPT
directly_supported_observations: User can instruct system to guide thinking (Socratic), explain in layers, check understanding, or use hints/quizzes/step-by-step
User specifies level: middle school, high school, college, beginner, or advanced
User can request: slow down, simpler language, analogy, deeper explanation, more advanced content
Documentation states 'there may be times when it gives a direct answer' - Socratic not always applied
Can upload files (notes, syllabus, worksheet, slides, textbook excerpt, problem photos) and reference specific sections
Memory feature saves learning goals, preferred explanation style, or topics studied before
Documentation explicitly states Study Mode 'does not replace your teacher, tutor, course materials' and 'can make mistakes'
design_implications: Pedagogical action selection requires explicit user instruction
Socratic questioning is opt-in feature, not default behavior
System adjusts based on explicit user feedback ('slow down', 'simpler') not automatic inference
Material grounding via file upload + manual section reference
Evidence collection sparse: observes completion and responses, does not infer mastery
limitations_and_non_inferences: No learning effectiveness claims provided
System does NOT automatically detect when to explain vs. hint vs. quiz
No learner modeling or knowledge state tracking described
Material constraint shallow: requires manual section pointing
Academic integrity boundaries unclear: 'Follow the AI-use policies of your school' - defers to external policy
sources.notes: Product documentation accessed 2026-07-29; document updated '23小时前' (23 hours ago) from access date

sources.title: Gemini 中的 LearnLM (LearnLM in Gemini)
directly_supported_observations: LearnLM built with education experts, optimized for learning based on rigorous research
Expert raters evaluated LearnLM against GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Gemini 1.5 Pro on pedagogical elements like guidance and correcting mistakes beyond mere accuracy
RCT in Sierra Leone: 1,763 middle school students (grades 7-8), 8 weeks, 12+ hours usage minimum
Effect: math performance from 50th to 64th percentile (a difference of 14 percentile ranks)
Effect equivalent to 1.8 to 2.5 additional years of learning progress
With appropriate system instructions, Gemini leverages LearnLM learning science research to trigger pedagogical behaviors
Multiple technical reports cited: May 2026, November 2025, December 2024, May 2024
design_implications: Learning effectiveness measurable via RCT methodology in specific context
Pedagogical quality evaluated as separate dimension from accuracy
Learning science principles can be embedded in LLMs via training
System instructions enable pedagogical behavior activation
Minimum engagement threshold exists: 12+ hours over 8 weeks for observed effect
limitations_and_non_inferences: RCT context specific: Sierra Leone middle school students, math subject, 8-week period
Generalization to other contexts (subjects, age groups, countries) requires caution
Implementation details not disclosed in product page
Comparison baseline not specified ('from 50th to 64th percentile' - compared to what control group?)
Technical reports referenced but not directly linked in product page
sources.notes: Chinese official Google Cloud page; RCT conducted with Fab AI partnership; percentile positions not percentage points

sources.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
sources.organization_or_authors: Rose E. Wang, Ana T. Ribeiro, Carly D. Robinson, Susanna Loeb, Dorottya Demszky
directly_supported_observations: RCT with 700+ tutors and 1,000+ students from underserved communities
Students with tutors using Tutor CoPilot 4 percentage points more likely to master math topics (p<0.01)
Gains highest for students of lower-rated tutors: 9 percentage points
Analysis of 350,000+ messages shows system increases probing questions and reduces generic praise
System cost: approximately $20/tutor/year
System models expert thinking to assist tutors in real time
Human-AI collaboration: AI assists tutors who then interact with students (not direct AI-student)
design_implications: Human-AI collaboration model validated via RCT in real-world educational setting
AI assistance to human tutors produces measurable learning gains
System bridges skill gaps: larger gains for lower-rated tutors (9 p.p.) vs. average (4 p.p.)
Specific pedagogical behaviors measurable at message level: probing questions increase, generic praise decreases
Economic viability consideration: $20/tutor/year cited explicitly
limitations_and_non_inferences: Domain-specific: math tutoring in underserved communities
Tutor-mediated interaction, not direct AI-student tutoring
Implementation details not disclosed: how 'expert thinking' is modeled and delivered
Rating mechanism for tutors not specified
Mastery definition not provided in Stanford page abstract
sources.notes: Stanford SCALE Initiative publication, November 2025; download available at scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/ai24_1054_v2.pdf

sources.title: ALEKS Knowledge Space Theory
sources.organization_or_authors: McGraw Hill ALEKS / Jean-Paul Doignon, Jean-Claude Falmagne
directly_supported_observations: Knowledge Space Theory applies combinatorics and stochastic processes to modeling specific knowledge domains
Algebra 1 example: approximately 350 basic concepts giving rise to millions of empirically feasible knowledge states
Adaptive assessment using Markovian procedures can gauge student knowledge state in 25-30 questions despite millions of possible states
System determines 'precisely what each individual student knows, and what the student is ready to learn next'
Authoritative source: Learning Spaces by Doignon & Falmagne (Springer-Verlag, 2011)
Each domain (e.g., Algebra 1, Algebra 2) requires separate pre-built knowledge structure
design_implications: Knowledge modeling feasible at scale: 350 concepts → millions of states, assessment remains tractable (25-30 questions)
Prerequisite relationships mathematically modelable via combinatorial framework
Adaptive assessment can be efficient using stochastic (Markovian) procedures
Domain specificity critical: each course requires separate knowledge structure
'Ready to learn' is computable from knowledge state and structure
limitations_and_non_inferences: Learning effectiveness not claimed: describes assessment framework, not learning outcomes
Pedagogical action selection not addressed
Knowledge state construction method not detailed in product page
'Empirically feasible' knowledge state definition not provided
Question selection algorithm not disclosed
Granularity tradeoff unclear: is 350 concepts for Algebra 1 the right level?
sources.notes: Official ALEKS product page; theoretical foundation in Knowledge Space Theory (Doignon & Falmagne); product actively used in K-12 and higher education
